opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. You know, a big part of it comes from a concern I've had for a while, which is that the current paradigm of generative AI is increasingly concentrated in the hands of a very small number of organizations. To build these frontier models you need enormous compute, enormous data, and enormous engineering resources, and that means most of the world, including most academic researchers, smaller companies, and many countries, end up being consumers of this technology rather than people who can really shape it, study it, or adapt it to their own needs.

So I'm drawn to small language models partly as a scientific question and partly as a values question. On the scientific side, I think there's an underexplored hypothesis that scale is not the only path to capability. When you look at how much data and compute these large models consume compared to how humans learn, it suggests there's a lot of inefficiency in the current recipe. If we can be much smarter about the data, through better curation, synthetic data generation, distillation, and better algorithms for reasoning, then I think smaller models can do surprisingly well on many tasks. Some of our work has shown that with the right kind of data and training approach, a much smaller model can match or even beat much larger ones on specific capabilities.

On the values side, if capable models can be small, then they can be open, they can run locally, they can be inspected and studied by researchers, and they can be customized for different languages, cultures, and communities whose needs aren't well served by one-size-fits-all models. That matters for privacy, for cost, for environmental footprint, and for pluralism, meaning AI that reflects many different perspectives rather than a single homogenized one.

So for me, democratizing generative AI isn't just about making it cheaper to use. It's about making sure that the ability to build, understand, and govern these systems is broadly distributed, and small language models feel like one of the most promising ways to get there.

r001.rationale: The response says frontier models require enormous resources and that small-model research is underexplored, but it does not state that exploration of scaling up received disproportionately more investment than exploration of small models.

r002.rationale: It says improved data and algorithms could help smaller models perform well, but does not argue that investing even a fraction of scaling-up resources could unlock substantially greater small-model capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you, it's great to be here. I think the simplest way to put it is that I don't want the future of AI to be something only a handful of organizations can build. Right now, if you want to create a truly capable model, the dominant recipe is to scale up: more data, more parameters, more compute, and that puts the frontier behind a wall that very few can get past. For a university lab, a startup, a researcher in a country without huge compute budgets, that is incredibly limiting. And I worry about what it means for science when the most interesting objects of study are things most scientists cannot actually touch, inspect, or reproduce.

So part of my motivation is almost a research-philosophy point. Scale works, but scale is also a bit of a brute-force answer, and I have always found it more intellectually satisfying, and frankly more important, to ask what the smarter path looks like. Can we get much more out of much less? What is it about the data, the training objective, the way we use inference-time computation, that matters most? Small models force you to confront those questions, because you cannot just throw more parameters at a problem and hope.

The other piece is that I genuinely believe small models can be surprisingly strong when you are thoughtful about them. Some of our work has shown that a carefully built small model can match or beat a much larger model on specific capabilities, whether that is commonsense reasoning, or summarization, or following certain kinds of instructions, if you are clever about how you generate and curate the training data and how you combine training with decoding-time methods. That has been a repeated lesson for me: a lot of the "intelligence" we attribute to scale is actually about the quality and shape of the knowledge the model sees, not just the raw quantity.

And there is a practical democratization angle too. Smaller models can run locally, on a laptop or a phone, which matters for privacy, for cost, for latency, for people who do not want their data going to a server somewhere. It means a teacher, a clinic, a small business can actually own and adapt their own model instead of renting intelligence from a giant provider. It also means more people can look inside, probe the failure modes, and study safety questions directly, which I think is essential if we want this technology to be trustworthy.

So for me these threads come together: better science, broader access, and a more pluralistic ecosystem where many people get to shape what these systems become, rather than just a few.

r001.rationale: The response says the dominant approach is scaling up and that its compute demands limit access, but it does not state that scaling research has received disproportionately more investment than small-model research.

r002.rationale: The response argues that small models can be capable with thoughtful data and methods, but it does not claim that investing a fraction of scaling resources could unlock substantially greater small-model capabilities.

astra-6.text:
For me, the question is whether we can make powerful AI accessible to more people—not just as something they can use, but as something they can study, build, and shape. If progress depends entirely on training ever larger models, then only a handful of organizations can really participate.

Small language models offer a different possibility. They require less compute, which can lower the cost of experimenting and adapting them to particular needs. That gives more researchers and communities a chance to contribute.

There’s also a scientific question that I find exciting: How much of what we get from scale could we achieve through better training methods and better data? I don’t think we should assume that making models bigger is the only way to make them better. Figuring out how to do more with less could help us understand intelligence while making the technology more broadly accessible.

r001.rationale: The response says large-model training can concentrate participation among a few organizations, but it does not state that exploration of scaling has received disproportionately more investment than exploration of small models.

r002.rationale: It says small models need less compute and could benefit from better methods and data, but does not argue that redirecting even a fraction of scaling resources could unlock substantially greater small-model capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, democratizing AI means that more people can participate in developing it, not just use a system built by a handful of companies. If progress requires ever larger models and enormous compute budgets, then universities and smaller research groups have very limited opportunities to contribute.

That’s why I’m interested in what we can achieve with smaller models through better training data and more efficient learning. Can we teach a model the capabilities we actually need, instead of assuming that scaling up is the only path? Smaller models can be less expensive to train, easier to study, and more practical to adapt to different needs. That opens up the possibility of a much broader community shaping where this technology goes.

r001.rationale: The response says that ever larger models require enormous compute budgets, but it does not state that research on scaling up has received disproportionately more investment than research on small models.

r002.rationale: The response describes potential benefits of better training data and more efficient learning for small models, but it does not argue that even a fraction of scaling resources could unlock substantially greater capabilities.
